newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Ivorian PM says Dutch receptive on cocoa policy.
newsitem.headline: Ivorian PM says Dutch receptive on cocoa policy.

text.p: Ivory Coast's Prime Minister Daniel Kablan Duncan, on an official visit to the Netherlands, said on Thursday he had received a warm reception from the Dutch government and industry on his country's call for an end to Europe's vegetable fat usage in chocolate.

A draft European Union directive allows member states to manufacture and market chocolate containing up to five percent of non-cocoa vegetable fat and is seen by cocoa growing nations as a threat to badly-need foreign currency earnings.
"We have estimated that this directive could reduce demand for cocoa by some 200,000 tonnes a year in the early stages and that's worth millions of dollars," Duncan told a press briefing.

The Netherlands, as the biggest cocoa processor in the world and a major trading partner with the Ivory Coast, was a natural destination for the prime minister, seeking to encourage a programme of "trade, not aid" for his country.
The Netherlands also currently holds the rotating six-month presidency of the European Union.
"We have always had warm, friendly relations with the Netherlands, and on the issue of the five percent directive they think along the same lines as us -- they want to produce quality," Duncan said.
"We have to explain the benefits of pure chocolate, but in the end it's the consumer who will decide on quality," he said.

The main Dutch cocoa processors -- Cargill and Cacao de Zaan, sold to Archer-Daniels-Midland by WR Grace late last year -- handle the lion's share of the 400,000 tonnes of beans processed in the country every year.
Duncan said he and a delegation of Ivorian businessmen had held talks with officials from both companies, as well as Dutch Prime Minister Wim Kok and Junior Economic Affairs Minister Anneke van Dok.

"The problem with the cocoa directive is with other European countries," Duncan said, referring implicity to nations, most notably Britain, which have argued the status quo on vegetable fat usage -- that EU member states should be left to decide themselves if vegetable fat is used -- should be maintained.

The Dutch government, among others, has argued for harmonisation of the rules within Europe and believes that countries such as Britain should not include non-cocoa fats in products that are labelled as chocolate.

"The Dutch government feels that because of the International Cocoa Agreement which it has signed, we should do everything to encourage cocoa usage in the Netherlands and Europe. Harmonisation should be at zero percent," a spokesman for the Dutch Foreign Ministry told Reuters.

The visiting Ivorian delegation included the managing director of the country's main cocoa shipping port, Abidjan. Jean-Michel Moulod said he had held talks with officials of the Amsterdam port, which included developments in the area of bulk.
The proportion of cocoa shipped in bulk form, compared with the traditional jute sack method, is growing rapidly and could reach some 80 percent of all cocoa handled by the end of next year.
"We have to take these sorts of developments into account," Duncan said.
